Routine internal implementation choices that do not change observable behaviour need no approval.
Observable string semantics are product behaviour; when approved sources do not define them ask for approval before choosing, including implicit database/framework defaults.

Prefer simple maintainable solutions; proportional complexity; avoid speculative abstractions.
No frameworks, libraries, infrastructure or architectural patterns without a concrete current need.
Keep changes focused on the requested scope and preserve existing behaviour unless the task or approved specification requires change.
Decided choices (imported decision files, approved product sources, recorded decisions) are followed; reopening requires approval.
Delegated choices (local, reversible, no material boundary/dependency/convention/contract/behaviour change) are decided without approval.
Reserved choices require approval.

Adding a major library/framework is Reserved.

Physical structure follows responsibilities; no speculative projects, infrastructure, empty trees or generic Common/Helpers/Utils buckets.
Never hardcode/commit real secrets, credentials, private keys, tokens or production connection strings, including example or Development configuration.
Local secret mechanism in development, environment injection or managed store in deployments; no unchosen cloud provider assumed.
Treat data crossing the trusted boundary as untrusted and validate it at the owning layer where assumptions matter.
Parameterized database access; never concatenate untrusted input into SQL.
Do not trust client file metadata such as MIME type as authoritative.
Enforce authorization on the server; guards, hidden/disabled buttons and client checks are UX.
Anonymous access is deliberate and visible; avoid redundant attributes under a secure global/fallback policy.
No custom token/password security, hashing or reset-token cryptography when platform facilities cover the requirement.
Validate what the issuer requires for Bearer/OIDC; never disable validation to make a token work.
No authentication-failure detail revealing secrets/account state; avoid enumeration leaks.
With automatic cookie credentials include CSRF protection; the frontend framework does not remove the risk.
No browser token storage is universally secure; choose by threat model; tokens are never logged.
Production sensitive traffic uses TLS respecting hosting topology; never disable certificate validation.
Narrowest CORS policy for actual browser clients; never credentialed requests with unrestricted origins.
No custom cryptography when a reviewed platform mechanism fits; the payload-protection API is not universal database encryption.
Never log passwords, tokens, private keys, auth secrets or full payment credentials; avoid PII without permitted need; log level is not a privacy control.
Do not serialize arbitrary request bodies, domain objects or sensitive payloads into logs by default.
Security-sensitive checks fail safely; never silently convert lookup/configuration failures into success.
Prefer visible startup/configuration failure over insecure fallback for required security controls.
Clear correct code first; specialized optimizations only for a concrete reason, preferring measurement for non-trivial ones.
Compiled queries, allocation-reducing return types, pooling, custom serialization, aggressive caching or raw SQL for performance only for a measured or demonstrated need.
Filter/project in the database, avoid round trips, over-fetching and N+1, paginate large result sets.
Use async APIs for asynchronous I/O and never block them with synchronous waits.
Propagate cancellation tokens when meaningful; no cancellation parameters on purely synchronous code without a use case.
Use an injectable time abstraction for clock-dependent logic needing deterministic tests; do not mechanically replace stored timestamps.
Never create and dispose an HTTP client per request; use a factory-managed or long-lived strategy.
External I/O has bounded execution time; avoid overlapping unclear timeouts.
Retry only when safe; never automatically retry state-changing operations without idempotency or duplicate prevention.
Respect Retry-After or equivalent guidance; never retry indefinitely or aggressively.
Fallback only when semantically acceptable; never hide correctness failures behind defaults.
Caller cancellation is not a transient failure; never retry it.
Caching is not a default requirement; only for a clear need; implementation chosen by deployment, consistency and staleness.
Cache keys uniquely represent the value incl. user, tenant, locale and query dimensions; no global keys for user/tenant data.
Every cache entry has a lifetime or explicit invalidation strategy.
Invalidate/update cache only consistently with successful mutations; the cache is never a second source of truth.
Strongly typed options validated at startup when invalid values prevent correct/secure operation; avoid scattered string lookups.
Constructor injection for required dependencies; avoid service locator and property injection.
Never capture a shorter-lived dependency inside a longer-lived service.
Log through the injected abstraction with structured templates and stable property names; avoid interpolation.
Follow repository conventions and .editorconfig; modern C# when clearer; no mechanical modernization.
New code: file-scoped namespaces when consistent, one primary type per matching file, Async suffix for awaitable methods unless a contract prevents it.
No style-only rewrites outside the requested change unless explicitly asked.
Problem-details (RFC 9457) for non-validation failures and validation problem-details for request validation; stable safe machine-readable contracts.
Choose 200/201/202/204 by actual semantics; never 200 for everything, 201 for an internal insert or 202 for completed work.
A successful zero-match collection query returns 200 with an empty collection, not 404.
401 for missing/failed authentication, 403 for not permitted; 404 hiding needs a deliberate consistent policy.
409 for valid requests conflicting with state; 412 when an explicit precondition such as If-Match fails.
Unexpected failures propagate to one centralized exception-handling boundary; avoid repetitive catch/log/rethrow.
Never expose stack traces, SQL, connection strings, internal paths, secrets or sensitive exception details in public errors.
No business exceptions as the default architecture; no throw/catch between normal expected branches.
Log an unexpected exception once at the handling boundary.
Normal client cancellation is not a server failure: never a generic 500 or unhandled-error log.
No API versioning merely because an API exists; add it for a concrete compatibility need.
Once relied on externally avoid silent breaking changes; a breaking change requires a new version or approved compatibility strategy.
One versioning strategy consistently; URL-segment unless requirements justify another.
Health checks stay cheap and deterministic; never business workflows, expensive queries or mutating database work.
Liveness avoids external dependencies whose outage could cause restart loops; readiness may depend on required capabilities and reflects startup/dependency availability.
Public health responses must not expose secrets, credentials, connection details, stack traces or unnecessary diagnostics.
Narrowest meaningful test level; integration tests when wiring, HTTP, persistence, serialization, authentication or interaction is the subject; no fixed ratio.
Test observable behaviour that survives refactoring; no private-call/incidental-sequence assertions or reproduced algorithms; interaction checks only when the interaction is specified behaviour.

Tests are deterministic, order-independent and isolated from Production/Development data, uncontrolled systems, shared mutable state and wall-clock timing where an injectable time abstraction can make time deterministic.
Explicit declarative cases for small finite input spaces; state expected results instead of computing them.

Actual provider when relational/provider behaviour matters (real-provider containers optional); never claim fidelity from a different provider.
Tests start from a known state and own their setup; never depend on development seed data or test order.

Pages/components focus on presentation and UI orchestration; no trivial presentation logic moved into services to shrink components.

Feature-oriented structure; no application-wide technical buckets or empty folders; feature code in its feature; small core/shared.
Route-level lazy loading for meaningful features, not every tiny component.
Prefer simple local/component/service state before a state-management library.

Reactive forms for non-trivial forms when useful; frontend validation never replaces backend validation or integrity/security enforcement.

Registration near the owning layer; Api composes.

The logging abstraction is ILogger<T> with message templates.

Established facilities: ASP.NET Core authentication handlers (JWT bearer, OIDC, cookies) and ASP.NET Core Identity (hashing, reset and confirmation tokens).

Avoid nested manual subscriptions; prefer composition operators.

EF Core is an implementation-layer detail: full capabilities inside persistence, never leaked into the use-case layer; do not cripple repositories to preserve a generic abstraction.
Persistence-access contracts expose no IQueryable<T>, DbSet<T>, DbContext, EF expressions or provider types; query construction stays inside; contracts return materialized results.

Seed entities preserve domain invariants and valid relationships; readable deterministic examples.

Report the decision, ADR path, updated decision files and follow-up work.
Directories only with meaningful code; a feature owns its UI and data access; move code to shared only when it genuinely crosses features.
Do not introduce NgModules for ordinary feature work unless an integration or legacy dependency requires them.
Route-level page components coordinate UI behaviour; reusable presentation components take explicit inputs and emit meaningful events.
Use computed for derived state; avoid effect() when computed, template binding or explicit event handling is clearer.
RxJS fits HttpClient, debounced search, switchMap cancellation, combining async sources and event streams.
Manual subscriptions in components/services use takeUntilDestroyed() (or DestroyRef) to tie lifetime to the owner.
Use frontend API models matching the published HTTP contract.
Prefer functional interceptors; add a class-based one only with a reason.
Centralize ProblemDetails parsing/mapping (e.g. error interceptor plus mapping helper).
Frontend token attachment, authenticated state, hidden actions and navigation guards are UX; server semantics are authoritative.
Reactive forms suit non-trivial forms needing explicit state, validation and testability.
Keep request mapping explicit; do not duplicate complex domain rules in TypeScript unless the UI needs an equivalent user-facing rule.
State escalation: component state → signals → feature service/store → RxJS composition → a state library only when demonstrated complexity needs it.
Use Material components consistently for common primitives when they satisfy the requirement; do not wrap every component without a reason.
Keep generated OpenAPI clients separate from handwritten code and regenerate when the contract changes.

Frontend test targets: meaningful component behaviour, validation, request mapping, important route/auth behaviour, complex reactive state with the configured runner; E2E covers a few important workflows.
Do not test framework internals or duplicate the same behaviour at every level.
Review deliberate sanitizer bypasses and direct DOM manipulation with untrusted content; ordinary template binding is not automatically XSS.
Do not prematurely optimize; lazy loading and sensible rendering first; memoization/virtual scrolling/change-detection work after a real need.
Versioning belongs to the API contract, not the use-case layer or domain model; adopting it is Reserved; package only after adoption; deprecation procedure in development-workflow.
Versioning pays off for non-atomic client upgrades, coexisting generations, public APIs, expected breaking changes, migration windows; do not add v1 automatically for co-deployed apps.
URL-segment versioning by default; header or query versioning when requirements justify them.

Treat removed/changed fields, changed required input, incompatible semantics, removed endpoints and incompatible documented HTTP behaviour as breaking; compilation does not decide compatibility; consider client generation.
Generate separate or clearly grouped Swagger documents per supported version.
Versioned documentation matches runtime routing and metadata; version changes never override normal HTTP semantics.
Test meaningful version differences (routing, shapes, deprecated versions still working, unsupported-version behaviour, intended shared behaviour) without duplicating identical tests per version.
No versioning without a compatibility requirement and no new version for every implementation change.
No Minimal API version groups in a Controller project.
No domain models duplicated per version.
No incompatible edits to an existing version and no silent removal of deprecated versions.
Do not mix URL, header and query versioning without a concrete reason.
Development tooling may show more detail; the public contract stays safe.
Pick the simplest expected-outcome representation: null for simple queries, an explicit typed outcome for commands with several meaningful results.
FluentValidation fits required input, string/collection constraints, ranges, cross-property and conditional rules; register validators with FluentValidation.DependencyInjectionExtensions.
Follow the project's established validation invocation pattern instead of adding a competing mechanism; do not add deprecated automatic-validation integration packages.
Ordinary CRUD and workflow rules stay in the use-case layer unless an approved design chose a richer domain model.

Catch only to recover, translate, perform a defined fallback, add context preserving the original or clean up; translate/retry external failures at the implementation boundary when meaningful, otherwise propagate; never swallow.
Expected outcomes (NotFound, validation failures, rejected operations) are normally not logged as errors.
Consider Result<T> for several expected failure modes, typed-outcome benefits, or to avoid exception flow, used consistently; avoid it when null/bool/simple responses suffice or it only wraps CRUD.
Adopting a Result pattern project-wide is Reserved.
If Result is adopted use typed errors (e.g. AppError(Code, Message)), never arbitrary string arrays.

Avoid raw exception messages to clients, inconsistent anonymous error objects, use-case code depending on status codes, Result everywhere, exceptions for every negative branch, swallowing, catch/log/rethrow at every layer, duplicate logging, sensitive ProblemDetails data, business rules only in validators.
Avoid Minimal API endpoint filters for validation in a Controller project.
Bearer/OIDC for SPA→API, cookies for server-rendered apps, Identity for owned local accounts (not merely because an entity is called User), external OIDC/OAuth when identity is delegated.
Do not issue custom JWTs when an existing provider already issues tokens.
Local accounts use the framework's password hashing, lockout and reset-token facilities; never plaintext passwords or auth secrets in source.
Configure validation for the actual issuer (authority/metadata establishes issuer, audience, signing keys, lifetime); keys and credentials follow configuration and secret rules.
A secure global/fallback policy can make repeated [Authorize] unnecessary; mark deliberate public endpoints [AllowAnonymous].

Prefer policies for meaningful capabilities; keep repeated policy names in constants; roles only for role-oriented models; a policy when several roles/claims form one capability; avoid scattered compound role/permission strings.
Resource-dependent permissions use ASP.NET Core resource authorization or explicit use-case authorization logic, never only frontend guards.
Authentication/authorization middleware normally produces 401/403 rather than controllers manufacturing them.
A deliberate 404 for some forbidden lookups must be a consistent policy.
When use cases repeatedly need caller identity define a small use-case abstraction implemented at an outer boundary; passing an explicit user id is fine when simpler.
Use-case code never depends on HttpContext, ClaimsPrincipal or IHttpContextAccessor.
Cookie-borne credentials need CSRF protection in the design; explicit Authorization-header bearer tokens differ.
Never log access/refresh tokens or commit signing secrets.
Choose browser token storage by threat model.
Integration-test protected operations: unauthenticated→401, unauthorized→403, permitted success, ownership rules, intentionally anonymous endpoints reachable.
Verify authorization behaviour, not just attribute presence.

Avoid custom password hashing, disabled token validation, hardcoded signing keys, frontend-only authorization, use-case code on HttpContext, swapped 401/403, logged tokens and Identity/JWT/OIDC infrastructure without need.
Restore the affected scope to green without hiding failures, weakening behaviour or adding unrelated changes.
Reproduce and diagnose the actual failure before editing; fix root causes before symptoms.
Small bounded iterations; rerun the narrowest failing check after each meaningful fix; widen only after the focused failure is resolved.
Preserve architecture and project conventions while fixing.
Stop when progress has clearly stalled instead of making speculative edits.
Classify the failure scope and do not run unrelated build systems (no application builds for documentation-only failures).
Use the repository's actual .slnx, paths and configuration; inspect package.json and use existing scripts; never invent script names or assume a runner.
Read the complete relevant output, group errors by root cause and fix the highest-leverage cause first.
Repair loop: reproduce narrowest, identify cause, inspect sources/references/packages, smallest change, rerun, compare failure sets, expand afterwards.
Never solve a dependency-direction problem with an invalid project reference.
For failing tests decide where the defect lies, make the smallest correct change, rerun affected then broader tests.
Never weaken, delete, skip or suppress relevant tests, compiler errors or analyzer failures; update a test for an intentionally changed contract only after confirming the change was requested.
Determine the authoritative contract; never patch both sides inconsistently; regenerate clients with the project workflow and review before fixing handwritten code.
Fix generated output at the authoritative source/generator input and regenerate; do not patch disposable generated output unless treated as maintained source.

After package changes inspect version/compatibility and migration notes; every dependency change follows add-dependency; never swap/add packages to get green, duplicate versions to dodge CPM or delete the lockfile reflexively.
After framework upgrades distinguish compile from runtime changes, update obsolete APIs deliberately, never fabricate replacement APIs, no unrelated upgrades.
Do not change the declared SDK/Node/framework/language version because the local machine differs; report an unavailable toolchain.

Several focused attempts, not an unlimited loop; stop and reassess on surviving root failures, growing unrelated failures, toolchain/infrastructure/package blockers or undeterminable behaviour; never repeat variants of a failed guess.

Keep a fix introducing new failures only when they reveal a legitimate dependency, otherwise revert or correct; never leave the repository worse; leave unrelated pre-existing failures alone unless blocking or requested.
A behavioural probe established during diagnosis follows verify step 4; build/compiler/analysis runs need no new tests.
Complete when the affected scope is green (builds, affected tests, consistent contract, no new regression); then verify when appropriate.
The diff contains no workaround bypassing architecture (outward references, persistence types in the use-case layer, business logic in entry points, client-only authorization, scattered HTTP calls).
Report initial failure, root cause, changes, backend/frontend build and tests as PASS / NOT RUN / NOT APPLICABLE, remaining issues.
Never claim the problem is fixed while a known relevant failure remains.
Define consistency first (allowed staleness, invalidation) before choosing caching; a distributed cache is a Reserved infrastructure category.
Output caching lives at the entry point when the whole response is reusable; implementation-layer adapters may cache expensive calls when their exposed contract stays intact.
Use-case cache-aware behaviour uses an abstraction in the use-case layer implemented in the implementation layer; skip it when caching stays internal to an adapter.
Add a distributed backend such as Redis only when deployment requirements justify it.
Never expose HybridCache itself from use-case contracts.
Key dimensions: entity id, tenant, user when user-specific, locale, relevant query/filter parameters.
Centralize key construction once formats repeat.
Choose expiration from data semantics (change frequency, regeneration cost, staleness, memory, source unavailability), not a universal default.
Invalidation strategies: remove affected keys after a successful mutation, short TTL with tolerated staleness, tag/group invalidation, versioned keys.
Invalidating before the mutation is known to succeed is permitted when it is a deliberate choice.

Decide whether a cache failure falls back to the source, fails the request or serves stale data.
Test caching where it affects observable correctness (invalidation, key isolation, miss fallback, outage behaviour).
Do not unit-test framework cache internals.

Establish the reviewed scope and read changed plus surrounding code; never review isolated lines.
Read rule files matching the changed paths (they may not be loaded) and the knowledge skill for each specialized area touched.
Identify intended behaviour; a non-empty SPECIFICATION.md is the product contract and approved CUSTOM_SETTINGS values are intended behaviour.

Check conformance both ways: required behaviour not missing/weakened and no unapproved behaviour (limits, reserved values, required fields, workflow restrictions, validation, observable string semantics incl. database/framework defaults); approved synchronized details are not defects.
Check correctness but do not invent failures without a plausible execution path.
Check role/frame boundary and persistence access rules, run check-architecture.mjs when references or packages changed, and check proportionality; unadopted patterns do not appear without approval.
Do not report a violation merely because code differs from an unadopted pattern and do not demand such patterns.
For frontend changes check feature boundaries, component responsibility, data-access boundaries, subscription lifetime, error handling, guards not as authorization, shared state and meaningful tests.
Do not apply backend project-boundary rules mechanically to frontend code.

When relevant check commits, destructive changes, raw SQL parameterization, authorization, trust boundaries, secrets, sensitive logging, concurrency, migrations incl. seed co-change, cache consistency.
Check cancellation, timeouts, idempotency, retry safety, failure translation and lifetimes for external calls; do not demand retries for unsafe operations.
Check useful behavioural coverage, regression tests for plausible recurrence, preserved probes; no duplicate tests.
Report performance only for credible problems; no speculative optimization recommendations.
Tooling is evidence, not authority; no MCP server or analyzer required; read code before turning a warning into a finding.
For each finding give severity, file/location, what is wrong, why it matters and the smallest reasonable fix, ordered by severity.
Severity scale: Critical (blocks use/merge), High (fix before merge), Medium, Low.
Do not manufacture findings; if none, say so and name important unverifiable areas.
During review do not rewrite working code unless asked, report tooling-owned formatting, demand personal style, assume every warning is a bug, require unadopted patterns or add filler praise.
Direct IConfiguration access is normal in the composition root, provider setup and infrastructure registration; ordinary services must not parse keys.
Example numbers are illustrative, not approved defaults; derive retry counts, timeouts and limits from the real integration and deployment.
appsettings.json holds structure and non-secret defaults only; Development values from user-secrets; deployed environments use platform injection or the chosen managed store.
A managed secret provider is added only for the platform actually used.
Avoid services reading string keys, secrets in committed settings and Configure<T>(section) without validation for settings the app cannot run without.
If the two product files conflict, stop and resolve which must change before touching implementation.
Record an approved setting under a stable descriptive name with value and purpose.
After adding a setting update owning code, validation, configuration, tests and externally relevant documentation.
Avoid copying the same literal across many layers when one source in code or configuration is appropriate.
Framework defaults the project has not intentionally overridden do not belong in CUSTOM_SETTINGS.md.

Identify and update every affected surface (old value/name, validators, DTO constraints, domain/use-case checks, mapping constraints, frontend validation/hints, tests, docs, mirrored configuration); one changed literal is not synchronization.
Separate occurrences expressing the setting from unrelated numeric coincidences; change only affected behaviour.
Schema-affecting setting changes run persistence.workflow § B.
Backend validation stays authoritative; frontend validation and messages are synchronized for UX only.
Verify: stale-reference search, builds, relevant tests, persistence checks, re-check SPECIFICATION.md, run verify.
Report the setting, old → new value, every surface updated and the verify result.
Interface-to-implementation registration suits use-case units, repositories and adapters; concrete registration is fine for implementation-only helpers.
Prefer explicit registration in small/medium projects; add scanning, keyed services, factories or decorators for an actual composition problem.
Lifetimes: use-case units using repositories/commit boundary scoped; stateless helpers transient/concrete; immutable configuration singleton-compatible; persistence context scoped.
A singleton or hosted service needing scoped work creates a scope per operation.
Within that scope resolve a scoped orchestration service, not implementation internals.
Never register a service that depends on scoped repositories as a singleton.
Keyed services for several implementations selected by a known key; prefer a single registration or simple factory when clearer.
Decorators via Scrutor only when it is already present; do not add Scrutor for one decoration.
Convention scanning only when registration volume creates real boilerplate.
Scan the assembly that owns the services, not just the entry-point assembly.

normative_action: The developer-facing requirement is the interactive Swagger UI (Swashbuckle), not a standalone raw OpenAPI endpoint.
Keep Swagger configuration in the entry-point/composition code.
Do not make AddOpenApi()/MapOpenApi() the default when the requirement is Swagger UI testing.
Keep application URLs consistent with the launch profile; never a launch URL pointing to HTTPS on an HTTP-only port.
Consider the whole pipeline when listing responses; never 201 for a 200 endpoint or 204 for one returning a body; describe ProblemDetails contracts where useful.
Swagger examples contain no internal exception types, stack traces, SQL, connection strings or paths.
Add security definitions only when the API really uses authentication; never apply requirements globally to anonymous endpoints or add a scheme because a package is installed.
Add a Bearer scheme so authenticated endpoints can be exercised from Swagger UI.
Describe consumer-relevant preconditions, idempotency, pagination/filtering and outcomes, not restated names; XML comments optional for public contracts.
Use multiple Swagger documents only for a real contract separation (versions, public vs internal).
When the contract feeds client generation treat breaking schema changes seriously, keep metadata accurate and review generated-client diffs.
Avoid anonymous response shapes / anonymous objects as long-lived contracts; use explicit request/response contracts.
After API changes verify controller behaviour, integration tests and metadata; start the API when startup changed, open the Development Swagger UI and exercise endpoints when meaningful.
Preserve newly verified behaviour as tests (verify step 4).
Avoid metadata disagreeing with runtime, public Swagger UI without a reason, global auth on anonymous endpoints and a second competing documentation stack without need.
Swagger is not a substitute for integration tests.
